blocks.text: 2.1 Demand-side analysis and market strategy
Concentration, seasonality and seats cap growth before demand does, and the base case meets the 1.8m inbound seat ceiling by 2030.
What was asked

The demand workstream was asked where Western Cape demand comes from, where growth will come from and how Wesgro should pursue it. The inception report framed the phase as a deep dive into priority markets to uncover growth levers from real-world demand and travel barriers (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p11).

It had two parts (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p15). Market assessments were to prioritise source markets by volume, spend and air access and profile the traveller types within them. Route-to-market analysis for India and China was to test visas, air connectivity and the visibility of Western Cape product on global channels.
The agreed report structure assigns this work to SLA Annexure B clauses 1.1.1, 1.1.7 and 3.2.3. [Clause wording to be checked against the signed Annexure B.]
What was done

Two decks carry the work. The Market Assessment Report of May 2026 set the baseline, the growth model, route to market and the traveller segments (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p2). The Demand-Side Analysis of June 2026 carried the model forward and added the African opportunity and the business-events landscape (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p26, p31).

Three methods supply the evidence (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p7). Skift's 2025 values-based survey covered more than 25,000 travellers in 34 outbound markets, 17 of them Wesgro priority markets, with 800 to 1,600 respondents a market (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p40). Desk review drew on Wesgro reports, Statistics South Africa and Google search data, and more than 20 stakeholder discussions added market-facing judgement (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p7).

The growth model builds a rate for each source market from four levers (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p18). They are outbound growth in the market, the Western Cape's penetration of it, the airlift ceiling and structural conditions such as currency and visas. It anchors on OAG aviation data for access and Skift traveller data for demand (p8). Its three scenarios vary the intervention, not the demand: "the difference between scenarios is not demand potential, but the extent to which structural barriers are removed" (p19).

The two decks print the same 2035 points from different bases. The May deck runs from a 2025 base of 1,498,829 and the June deck from a 2024 base of 1,445,031 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20). This report uses the 2025 base and logs the difference.

The Current State Diagnostic of December 2025 supplied the baseline folded in here: source-market concentration, the seasonal profile and the first segment work (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p16 to p20, p29, p32). Its figures are cited where they add to the later decks.
Findings that survived into the tree

**1. Five markets carry the province.** The UK, Germany, the USA, the Netherlands and France supplied 63% of overseas arrivals in 2025, and the first three alone 52% (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p13). The same slide prints 61% in its text; the report uses 63%, the sum of the printed shares. The December baseline showed the same pattern, with the top five at 61% of Cape Town overseas air arrivals from January to August 2024 (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p29).

Those markets also pay the most. Average spend per visitor in 2024 ran from R32,900 for the USA and R26,500 for the UK down to R8,600 for Namibia and R8,500 for Zimbabwe (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p14). The deck's own reading is that high-spend visitors come from Europe and North America, "tying future value growth to slower-growing source markets" (p14).

**2. Six months carry nearly two thirds of the year.** December, January and November were the peak months of 2025 at 12.7%, 11.5% and 11.3% of overseas visitors, while June fell to 6.1% (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12). October to March hold about 65% on that table, a provisional figure because its twelve shares sum to 104.9%. On a Cape Town overseas air-arrivals basis for January to August 2024 the split was 61% and 39% (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p25).

The deck draws the conclusion that matters for strategy. Growth depends on "improving conversion in Apr-Sep rather than pushing incremental demand into already busy peak months" (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p25).

**3. Demand supports 2.18m to 2.52m arrivals by 2035.** From the 2025 base, the model projects 1,822,634 arrivals in the conservative case, 2,175,778 in the base case and 2,516,282 in the accelerated case, implied growth of 2.0%, 3.8% and 5.3% a year (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19). The step from base to accelerated rests on confirmed direct routes to India and China, above-baseline activation and more hub capacity into Cape Town (p18). The model states the dependency plainly: "without confirmed routes, volume reverts to base" (p19).

blocks.caption: The base case passes the 1.8m inbound seat ceiling at the 2030 year point, and only the accelerated case reaches 2.5m by 2035.
blocks.source: Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19 (scenario end points) and p20 (base-case year points and the seat ceiling as drawn). OAG Aviation Analytics.

chart.footnote: The conservative and accelerated cases are printed as 2025 and 2035 points only and are drawn as straight lines between them.

blocks.text: In the base case the hubs add the most arrivals and the acceleration markets grow fastest. Between 2025 and 2035 hub markets add 206,584 arrivals, mature markets 178,780, acceleration markets 175,818, regional markets 110,298 and Japan and South Korea 5,469 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20, computed). India more than doubles from 76,547 to 165,260 and China with Hong Kong from 43,412 to 92,598, both at 8% a year (p22).

blocks.caption: Hub and acceleration markets supply 382,402 of the 676,949 arrivals the base case adds between 2025 and 2035.
blocks.source: Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20. Groups as printed: Mature (UK, Germany, USA, Netherlands, France, Switzerland); Hubs (UAE, Ethiopia, Qatar, Turkey); Regional (Namibia, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana, Kenya and others); Acceleration (Gulf, China, India, Brazil); Strategic (Japan, South Korea).

blocks.text: Spend follows the mix. At fixed average spend per group, from R24,500 a visitor in mature markets to R8,500 in regional ones, base-case foreign spend rises from a modelled R27.12bn in 2024 to R40.59bn in 2035 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p24).

**4. Seats bind before demand does.** The model draws current air access as "a hard ceiling at 1.8 million inbound seats", and the base case first passes it at the 2030 year point with 1,802,929 arrivals (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20). Only six year points are printed, so the crossing falls between 2028, at 1,673,855, and 2030. The deck judges 2.1 million by 2035 achievable only with deliberate intervention to add capacity (p20).

**5. Four segments fit the province, and each has a home market.** Skift's survey identifies four values-based segments most aligned with the Western Cape, together about 97 million addressable travellers (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p41 to p43). The deck marks the pairs to pursue: Curious Explorers in the UK and the USA, Creative Connectors in India, Discerning Connoisseurs in China and the UAE and Reflective Adventurers in Germany (p43). Curious Explorers and Discerning Connoisseurs are "most aligned to the Western Cape's offering" (p4).

blocks.caption: Four segments hold about 97 million addressable travellers, and the deck pairs each with the markets where it is most concentrated.
blocks.source: Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p42, p43, p45, p48, p51, p54. Priority pairs are the cells highlighted on p43. Trip spend is average long-haul trip spend as printed; the currency is not named on the slides.
rows: Cultural immersion, learning and authentic connection

blocks.text: The segments matter for spread as much as for volume. Curious Explorers offer the "strongest opportunity for geographic dispersal beyond Cape Town", and Reflective Adventurers have "strong potential to support seasonality mitigation" through year-round outdoor and wellness travel (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p56).

**6. India and China already arrive, through other carriers' hubs.** An estimated 71,000 travellers fly from India to Cape Town each year through connecting hubs and about 30,000 from China, together about 101,000 journeys (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p46, p48, computed). Addis Ababa and Dubai handle more than 80% of the Indian connections, and direct Indian service is "unlikely before 2030 due to aircraft constraints at Air India and IndiGo" (p48).

The barriers are named market by market (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p51). Chinese and Gulf travellers face slow, document-heavy visa processes; India has no direct flight to Mumbai or Delhi and thin Indian-friendly adaptation; the Gulf lacks Arabic-language booking and local-currency pricing.

Each market books through its own platforms. Chinese travellers discover on Douyin and Xiaohongshu and book on Trip.com, Qunar and Fliggy; Indian travellers book through MakeMyTrip, Booking.com and Expedia; much Gulf travel still runs through private advisors and concierge agencies (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p45, p47, p49; Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p34, p35). The deck's prescription is to activate inside those platforms and shift investment "toward trade-led conversion rather than broad awareness campaigns" (p55).

**7. Africa is a base and a growth market at once.** The Western Cape recorded 323,971 tourist arrivals from 16 reported African markets in 2024, 62% of them from Zimbabwe and Namibia (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p27). African visitors spent R4.2bn in the province in 2025, with Nigerians and Ghanaians spending most per visit at R31,000 and R27,700 (p29). Skift models Nigeria's addressable market at 310,000 to 510,000 adult trips a year and Kenya's at 240,000 to 400,000 (p28, p30).

The sources rank Ghana differently. The Demand-Side Analysis names Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana as priority markets (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p30), while Skift's memo places Ghana among its fourth-tier watch markets for brand seeding rather than conversion (Skift African Market Analysis memo, Mar 2026, section 2). Regional markets also steady the year: Namibia and Zimbabwe "add stability, repeat demand and counter-seasonal volume" (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p14).

**8. Business events are the strongest green-season lever.** International association meetings in Cape Town rose from 33 in 2022 to 58 in 2024, and 109 of the 136 meetings held over the three years fell between May and November (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p37, computed). Cape Town ranked 35th in the 2024 ICCA ranking and hosted 37 of South Africa's 64 UIA-recorded meetings in 2025 (p36, p38). Cape Town hotel occupancy was 53% in June 2023, the gap such events fill (p34).

The deck warns against a single target. Meetings, incentives, conventions and exhibitions have different buyers and lead times, and only conferences are measured well; meetings are "absent from consolidated provincial statistics" (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p35, p36). Stellenbosch and George are named as credible secondary hubs, with delegates spending extra nights in the regions while major events stay in Cape Town (p41).

blocks.title: What this means for the tree
paras: **Validates FA01, Respond to growth segment traveller preferences.** Four segments, each with named home markets (finding 5).

**Supports FA02, Create green-season demand with MICE and events.** Business events cluster from May to November, when leisure demand is weakest (findings 2 and 8). The seat side of the case sits in 2.2.
**Supports FA03, Make the whole province findable and bookable.** Conversion runs through market-specific platforms that Western Cape product must reach (finding 6).
**Rewords FA04, Convert India and China hub traffic.** About 101,000 hub journeys a year and no direct Indian route before 2030 (finding 6).
**Validates FA05, Increase yield in mature markets.** The highest-spending visitors come from the slowest-growing markets (findings 1 and 3).
**Validates FA06, Build a regional foundation (Africa).** A large regional base and two high-yield growth markets (finding 7).

**Supplies the binding constraint for FA07, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes,** and the visa barriers for **FA19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits** (findings 4 and 6).
